cards.prompt: Easy to guess, or hard to guess?
cards.explanation: Names, birthdays, common patterns and short symbol swaps are guessed first. Four random words are long and unpredictable.

cards.prompt: Make an all-lowercase password last **at least a million years**.
cards.explanation: Around **16 lowercase letters** gets past a million years. Every letter multiplies the time by 26.

cards.prompt: Your aunt needs a new passphrase for her email. Which is best?

options.text: To be or not to be, that is the question

cards.explanation: Four **random** words are long and unpredictable. A famous quote is in guessing lists, and symbol swaps on a common word are tried early.

cards.prompt: A shopping site was hacked. You used that password for your email and music app too.

choices.text: Change your email password to a new one
choices.consequence: Your email can reset everything else, so it comes first. Then give the others their own new passwords.
Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites quickly.

choices.text: Change all three to one new password
choices.consequence: Then one leak opens all three again.

cards.explanation: Change the reused password everywhere, starting with **email**, and give every account its own password.

cards.prompt: A stranger has your email password, but your email uses an authenticator app too. Can they get in?

options.text: No: they'd also need the code from your phone
Yes: a stolen password is all anyone needs
Yes: two-step only stops people guessing passwords

cards.explanation: No. The password is only half of it: they'd also need the code from the app on **your** phone.

cards.prompt: "I'm from the game's support team. Tell me the code we just texted you." What is this?

options.text: A scam: nobody real asks for your sign-in code
Real support: they need it to check it's really you
Safe, as long as they already know your username

cards.explanation: No real company ever asks for a sign-in code. Anyone who does is trying to get into your account.

cards.prompt: Whose email is **hardest** to break into?

steps.text: Four friends protect it in different ways.

choices.consequence: Right. A passkey is the strongest way to sign in, and fake sites can't use it.
That's strong, but one way to sign in is stronger still, and fake sites can't use it.
Better than a password alone, but text codes are the weakest second proof.

choices.text: Dev: a long passphrase, nothing else
choices.consequence: A great passphrase, but with no second proof, one leak is enough to get in.

cards.explanation: Strongest first: a **passkey**, an **authenticator app**, then a **text code**. A password alone, however long, has no second lock.
